newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Jospin face-to-face with crime issue.
newsitem.headline: France's Jospin face-to-face with crime issue.

text.p: Socialist leader Lionel Jospin came face-to-face with one of the deep anxieties of the French public -- rising street crime -- as he toured a troubled Paris outer surburb during France's election campaign on Thursday.

Fellow Socialist Dominique Lefebvre, mayor of this sprawling commuter surburb of over 50,000 people, told Jospin the "feeling of impunity among (delinquent) youths and accompanying feeling of insecurity in the rest of the population can only work in favour of the (extreme rightist) National Front.
"We need more police, more judges, stricter punishments and a more open ear for the victims," Lefebrvre told Jospin who was on his first day of public campaigning in the snap parliamentary election.
Lefebvre said it was a mistake to ignore the law-and-order issue which has strongly fuelled the rise of Jean-Marie Le Pen's NF party among the French lower and lower-middle classes.

The mayor, whose town's population includes 15 percent of foreigners and nearly an equal number of youths of foreign origin with French passports, said strong efforts should be made to integrate them into mainstream society.
One 'beur' (French youth of North African origin) to whom a friend of mine spoke to about 'citizenship' replied he thought the word came from the FN vocabulary," Lefebvre lamented.
Le Pen's party has singled out youths of foreign origin, especially Arabs and black Africans, as being disproportionately involved in street crime and wants to expel millions.
Jospin, a professorial figure who has spent his life in protected surroundings, looked askance when taken aboard the local 445 bus line notorious among local residents for attacks on its drivers.

Pushed to the back of the bus by a crush of television crews, Jospin found himself cheek-by-jowl with 16-year-old Kemal Dursun, born in Istanbul but who arrived in France with his parents when he was two years old.
"Ca va?, (all o.k.)" Jospin said tentatively. "Ca va," replied the black-leather-jacketed youth before an embarrassed silence set in again.
Dursun told reporters he lived in the rough St.Christophe area of Cergy "where the police hassle the youths, the youths harass the police and no one dares to go out after 10 p.m."
Jospin only relaxed when he got off the bus and encountered a group of little girls whose forenames, Claire, Fatima, Lucy and Sarah, indicated their diverse origins.
Learning they were starting the last year of primary school, Jospin, a former education minister, lectured them paternally on the need to work very hard before entering junior high school.

Jospin later told a rally of local residents that the centre-right government was to blame for rising crime since an inordinate number of police were used to guard government buildings or confront demonstrations rather than being in the streets preventing crime.
He said his Socialist party would order the hiring of 35,000 youths from troubled areas to act as big brother-type crime preventers if it won the May 25-June 1 election.
